shortTheory.question: What changes in velocity can a force produce?
shortTheory.answer: As velocity is a vector quantity, so the change may be in its magnitude, direction or in both of them.

shortTheory.question: State Newton's first law of motion.
shortTheory.answer: A body continues its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by some external force.

shortTheory.question: Define impulse of force.
shortTheory.answer: When a large force F acts on an object for a short interval of time, the impulse of the force is defined as the total change in momentum of the object.

shortTheory.question: Why are you pushed back into your seat when a car suddenly accelerates from rest?
shortTheory.answer: On the other hand, when the bus starts moving quickly from rest, the passengers are pushed back against the seat. This time, the tendency of passengers is to retain their state of rest.

shortTheory.question: Define terminal velocity.
shortTheory.answer: This constant velocity achieved by an object is called its terminal velocity.

shortTheory.question: State the principle of conservation of momentum.
shortTheory.answer: If no external force acts on an isolated system, the final total momentum of the system is equal to the initial total momentum of the system.

shortTheory.question: Give five examples of contact forces.
shortTheory.answer: Friction, drag, thrust, normal force and air resistance.

definitions.text: A common concept of a force is a push or a pull that starts, stops or changes the magnitude and direction of velocity of a body.
A contact force is a force that is exerted by one object on the other at the point of contact.
It is the force that resists motion when the surface of one object comes in contact with the surface of another.
The drag force is the resistant force caused by the motion of a body through a fluid. It acts opposite to the relative motion of any object moving with respect to surrounding fluid.
It is an upward force exerted by a liquid on an object immersed in it.
It is the force of reaction exerted by the surface on an object lying on it. This force acts outward and perpendicular to the surface. It is also called the support force upon the object.
It is the resistance (opposition) offered by air when an object falls through it.
It is the force experienced by a rope when a person or load pulls it.
It is a force that brings certain materials back to their original shape after being deformed.
A non-contact force is defined as the force between two objects which are not in physical contact.

Every object in the universe attracts every other object with a force that is directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. This is known as Newton's law of gravitation.

There are four fundamental forces in nature. These are:

1. Gravitational force
2. Electromagnetic force
3. Strong nuclear force
4. Weak nuclear force
A body continues its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by some external force.
Force is an agency which changes or tends to change the state of rest or of uniform motion of a body.
The property of a body to maintain its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line is called inertia.

If a net external force acts upon a body, it accelerates the body in the direction of force. The magnitude of acceleration is directly proportional to the magnitude of force and is inversely proportional to the mass of the body.
One newton is the force which produces an acceleration of 1 m s⁻² in a body of mass 1 kg.

For every action, there is always
an equal and opposite reaction.

If one body exerts a force on a second body,
the second body also exerts an equal and
opposite force on the first body.
The characteristic of a body which determines the magnitude of acceleration produced when a certain force acts upon it is known as mass of the body.
The weight of an object is equal to the force with which the Earth attracts the body towards its centre.
The gravitational field is a space around a mass in which another mass experiences a force due to gravitational attraction.
The gravitational field strength is defined as the gravitational force acting on unit mass.
This opposing force is the static friction F_s.
When the block is sliding, friction still exists. It is known as kinetic friction.
This constant velocity achieved by an object is called its terminal velocity.
When an object rolls over a surface, the friction produced is called rolling friction.
The momentum of a moving body is the product of its mass and velocity.
When a large force F acts on an object for a short interval of time, the impulse of the force is defined as the total change in momentum of the object.

definitions.term: Newton's second law in terms of momentum
definitions.text: The rate of change of momentum of a body is equal to the force acting on it.
If no external force acts on an isolated system, the final total momentum of the system is equal to the initial total momentum of the system.

w = m × g  (w in N, m in kg, g in m s⁻² or N kg⁻¹)
formulas.use: Find an object's weight from its mass and local gravitational field strength.

formulas.formula: g = w ÷ m  (g in N kg⁻¹ or m s⁻², w in N, m in kg)
formulas.use: Find gravitational field strength from weight and mass.

formulas.formula: F = m × a  (F in N, m in kg, a in m s⁻²)
formulas.use: Find the net force, mass or acceleration using Newton's second law.
Convert between the newton and its SI base units.

formulas.formula: a = Δv ÷ Δt = (v_f − v_i) ÷ Δt  (a in m s⁻², velocities in m s⁻¹, Δt in s)
formulas.use: Find average acceleration from the change in velocity and time.

formulas.formula: v_f = v_i + a × t  (velocities in m s⁻¹, a in m s⁻², t in s)
formulas.use: Find final velocity or time when acceleration is constant.

formulas.formula: p = m × v  (p in kg m s⁻¹ or N s, m in kg, v in m s⁻¹)
formulas.use: Find the momentum of a moving object.

formulas.formula: F × Δt = m × Δv = m × (v_f − v_i) = Δp  (F in N, Δt in s, m in kg, velocities in m s⁻¹, Δp in kg m s⁻¹ or N s)
formulas.use: Find impulse or the change in momentum during a force acting for a time.

formulas.formula: F = Δp ÷ Δt = m × (v_f − v_i) ÷ Δt  (F in N, Δp in kg m s⁻¹, Δt in s, m in kg, velocities in m s⁻¹)
formulas.use: Find average force from the rate of change of momentum.

formulas.formula: m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = m₁v′₁ + m₂v′₂  (masses in kg, velocities in m s⁻¹, momentum in kg m s⁻¹)
formulas.use: Apply conservation of momentum to two objects before and after an interaction.

formulas.formula: m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = (m₁ + m₂)v  (masses in kg, velocities in m s⁻¹)
formulas.use: Find the shared velocity when two objects stick together after collision.

formulas.formula: v₂ = −(m₁ × v₁) ÷ m₂  (masses in kg, velocities in m s⁻¹)
formulas.use: Find recoil velocity when a stationary gun-object system separates; the minus sign shows opposite direction.

fullMarks: For a law or definition, write the complete statement accurately; for Newton's laws and conservation of momentum, do not leave out conditions such as 'net external force' or 'isolated system'.
For numericals, write the given data first, convert all quantities to SI units, state the formula, substitute values with units, and give the final answer with its unit.
For momentum and recoil problems, choose a positive direction and keep velocity signs consistent; show that a negative answer means motion in the opposite direction.
In force questions, use the net/resultant force in F = ma, and make clear which object each force acts on.
For impulse and momentum-change questions, show the initial and final velocities and calculate Δv as v_f − v_i; include the contact time when calculating force.
For conservation-of-momentum problems, write total momentum before = total momentum after before substituting numbers.
For a free-body diagram, represent the object clearly, draw force arrows from it, point each arrow in the correct direction, and label every force.
End explanation answers with a direct conclusion that links the physical idea to the situation—for example, increased stopping time means less average force for the same change in momentum.

mistakes: Writing a mass in newtons or a weight in kilograms loses marks. Use kg for mass and N for weight.
Using the mass in grams directly in a formula: convert grams to kilograms first, such as 5 g = 0.005 kg.
Treating action and reaction as forces that cancel on one object. They act on different objects; identify the object each force acts on.
Leaving out the minus sign in recoil or collision calculations. Choose a direction as positive and explain that a negative velocity means the opposite direction.
Using the applied force instead of the net force in F = ma. Account for opposing forces when they are present.
For impulse problems, using v_i − v_f instead of v_f − v_i or forgetting the time interval when finding force. Write the signed change in velocity carefully.
Saying that terminal velocity means the object has stopped. It is still falling, but at constant velocity because air resistance balances its weight.
